entries.topicDescription: Functional-style operations over collections with the Stream API and lambda expressions.

tips.title: Streams are lazy — nothing runs until a terminal operation
tips.content:
Calling .filter() or .map() on a stream doesn't actually
process any elements. It just builds up a pipeline description.
Nothing happens until a terminal operation — collect(),
forEach(), count(), reduce() — is called.

This matters for two reasons. First, an intermediate stage
like filter() only ever sees the elements that survive the
stages before it, processed one at a time end-to-end, not in
separate passes. Second, a stream with no terminal operation
does nothing at all — a common source of "why didn't this run"
bugs.

Because streams are lazy and single-use, you cannot reuse a
stream after a terminal operation has consumed it — calling
any method on it again throws IllegalStateException.

tips.title: Method references are a shorthand for single-expression lambdas
tips.content:
When a lambda just forwards its argument to an existing method,
a method reference (Class::method) says the same thing with
less noise and is usually easier to read at a glance.

There are four forms: a static method (Integer::parseInt), an
instance method on a particular object (System.out::println),
an instance method on an arbitrary object of a type (that's
what String::toUpperCase is above — the first stream element
becomes the receiver), and a constructor (ArrayList::new).

Method references aren't just cosmetic — the compiler resolves
them to the exact same functional-interface target as an
equivalent lambda, so there's no performance difference, only
a readability one.

tips.title: Collectors.groupingBy powers SQL-like aggregation
tips.content:
Collectors.groupingBy(classifier) partitions a stream into a
Map<K, List<T>> keyed by whatever function you give it — the
functional-programming equivalent of SQL's GROUP BY.

Pass a second, "downstream" collector to aggregate each group
instead of just collecting it into a list — counting(),
summing, averagingInt(), or even a nested groupingBy() for a
multi-level breakdown.

This single collector replaces what would otherwise be a
hand-rolled loop building up a HashMap<K, List<V>> — correct,
but easy to get subtly wrong (forgetting computeIfAbsent, for
instance) compared to one declarative call.
